capital: Sri Jayawardenepura Kotte (legislative capital) / Colombo (commercial capital)
summary: An island nation in the Indian Ocean south of India, formerly called Ceylon, known for black tea, Buddhist heritage sites and cultural diversity. It became independent from Britain in 1948.

ranking.name: Buddhism
ranking.description: Buddhism was introduced in the 3rd century BCE by Mahinda, son of Emperor Ashoka, and the Anuradhapura Kingdom made it the state religion. For more than two thousand years afterward Buddhism was closely bound up with Sinhalese kingship, and the Tooth Relic of the Buddha became a symbol of royal authority. Buddhism declined for a time during the colonial period, but the Buddhist revival movement of the late 19th century combined it with anti-colonial Sinhalese nationalism; the 1972 constitution gave Buddhism the foremost place. Its followers are mainly Sinhalese, living in the south, center and west.

ranking.name: Hinduism
ranking.description: Hinduism was brought by Tamils who migrated from southern India over thousands of years, and the Jaffna Peninsula in the north was once the center of a Tamil kingdom. In the 19th century the British colonial rulers also recruited large numbers of Tamils from southern India to work on tea plantations in the central highlands, so Hindus are concentrated in the north, the east and the central tea-growing region.

ranking.name: Islam
ranking.description: Islam arrived from the 8th century onward with Arab traders, who intermarried with locals to form the "Moor" community, which mainly speaks Tamil and is found in coastal cities of the east and west. There are also groups such as Malays and Indian Muslims. After the 2019 Easter attacks, the Muslim community suffered retaliatory violence.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: In the 16th century the Portuguese established bases on the coast of Sri Lanka and spread Catholicism among fishermen and coastal residents, and many converts adopted Portuguese surnames. After the Dutch replaced the Portuguese in the 17th century they suppressed Catholicism for a time, but the faith survived in the coastal regions, and today Catholics are found among both Sinhalese and Tamils.

ranking.name: Other Christianity
ranking.description: The Dutch East India Company promoted Reformed Protestantism in the 17th–18th centuries, and during British rule in the 19th century Anglican, Methodist and Baptist missionaries founded schools and trained a Westernized elite. But the number of converts to Protestantism has always been limited, and in recent years the expansion of Pentecostal churches has provoked resentment among Buddhist groups.

religion.background: In the 3rd century BCE, Mahinda, son of the Mauryan emperor Ashoka of India, brought Buddhism to Sri Lanka, and the Anuradhapura Kingdom soon made it the state religion. Sri Lanka became an important center of Theravada Buddhism, and the Pali Canon was committed to writing here around the 1st century BCE. Hinduism arrived in the north and east with the migration and invasions of southern Indian Tamils. Islam arrived in the Middle Ages with Arab traders. From the 16th century the Portuguese, Dutch and British successively colonized the island, bringing Catholicism and Protestantism. After independence in 1948, Buddhism was given "foremost place" in the 1972 constitution, and conflict between Sinhalese Buddhist nationalism and the Tamils led to the civil war of 1983–2009.

language.official: The official languages are Sinhala and Tamil, and English is the link language.

ranking.name: Sinhala
ranking.description: Sinhala is the language of the Sinhalese, Sri Lanka's largest ethnic group, and according to legend it originated with Prince Vijaya, who crossed the sea from northern India in the 5th century BCE. It absorbed many words from the Pali Buddhist scriptures and has a distinctive rounded script. The 1956 Sinhala Only Act made it the sole official language, and it remains the main language of the government and of the south and central regions.

ranking.name: Tamil
ranking.description: Tamil is spoken by the Tamils of northern and eastern Sri Lanka, the Indian Tamils of the central tea plantations, and most Muslims. The 1956 Sinhala Only Act put Tamils at a disadvantage in public employment and education and intensified ethnic conflict; Tamil became an official language only after the 13th Amendment to the constitution in 1987, but the civil war did not end until 2009.

language.history: Sinhala belongs to the Indo-Aryan branch of the Indo-European language family and is generally thought to have been brought by migrants from northern India around the 5th century BCE; it has absorbed influences from Pali, Sanskrit and Tamil, and its script derives from the ancient Indian Brahmi script. Tamil belongs to the Dravidian family and has long been used in the north and east along with migrants from southern India. During the colonial period English became the language of the elite. In 1956 the Bandaranaike government passed the Sinhala Only Act, making Sinhala the sole official language, which provoked strong resentment among Tamils and became one of the major causes of the later civil war. After a constitutional amendment in 1987, Tamil was also made an official language, with English as the link language.

ranking.name: Kiribath (milk rice)
ranking.description: A creamy white rice cake made by cooking rice with coconut milk and cut into diamond shapes, often eaten with spicy coconut sambol (lunu miris).
ranking.history: Kiribath means "milk rice" and symbolizes auspiciousness and prosperity in Sinhalese culture. It is the first food eaten on the morning of the Sinhala and Tamil New Year each April. It is also prepared on the first day of each month, at weddings, at a baby's first month and on other occasions to bring good luck. Sri Lanka has grown rice and coconuts since ancient times, and the combination of these two most important products has become the most representative festive food.

ranking.name: Kottu roti
ranking.description: Roti flatbread is chopped and stir-fried on a griddle with vegetables, egg, meat and curry sauce; as it is made, the knives clatter rhythmically against the griddle.
ranking.history: Kottu is a fairly young dish. It is generally thought to have originated in the 1970s in Batticaloa in eastern Sri Lanka, or in snack shops of the Tamil and Muslim communities in the south, made from leftover roti. In the 1980s–90s it became popular across the country, and the "clang-clang" of two metal blades chopping kottu at roadside stalls in the evening is a representative street sound of Sri Lankan cities.

ranking.name: Hoppers (appa)
ranking.description: A bowl-shaped thin pancake cooked in a small round pan from fermented rice batter and coconut milk, with a crisp edge and a soft center, and sometimes an egg. It is often eaten with coconut sambol or curry, or fried with an egg cracked into the middle.
ranking.history: Appa is a traditional dish shared by Sri Lanka and the Indian state of Kerala, made from the two most basic products, rice and coconut. The English name "hopper" is a corruption of appa from the British colonial period. It is often eaten for breakfast or dinner, and a sweet version is also made at New Year and festivals; it is an everyday food in Sri Lankan homes and snack shops.

ranking.name: String hoppers (indiappa)
ranking.description: Rice flour dough is pressed into fine strands and steamed into small round nests, eaten with curry, coconut sambol or lentil soup. They are soft and mild in taste and often eaten for breakfast.
ranking.history: Indiappa (string hoppers) share their origin with South India's idiyappam, and probably came with the frequent exchange of people and culture between southern India and Sri Lanka in ancient times. Making them requires a special mold to press out the fine strands, so they are a rather laborious home food, often eaten for breakfast. Throughout Sri Lanka it is a traditional rice dish that appears both on ordinary days and at festivals.

ranking.name: Lamprais (Dutch Burgher rice parcel)
ranking.description: Rice is baked wrapped in a banana leaf together with side dishes such as several curries, meatballs, fried eggplant and shrimp paste. After baking, the rice absorbs the aroma of the banana leaf and the curries, giving a rich flavor.
ranking.history: Lamprais comes from the Dutch word lomprijst ("a packet of rice") and is a dish of the Burgher community (descendants of Dutch and Portuguese) left over from the Dutch colonial period (1658–1796). It combines Dutch meatballs, Portuguese influence and Sri Lankan curries, showing a cuisine of multicultural blending from the colonial era. Today it is still the Sunday feast of Burgher families and is also sold in restaurants in Colombo.
